meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Resolve to be tender with the young, compassionate with the aged, sympathetic with the striving, and tolerant of the weak and the wrong. Sometime in life you will have been all of these'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Buddha. This exact line was written by Parade columnist Lloyd Shearer (“Walter Scott”), first published 30 December 1973.

answer.label: Not Gautama Buddha — actually Lloyd Shearer
answer.authorDates: 1916–2001 · American celebrity columnist, “Walter Scott’s Personality Parade”
answer.sourceLine: The exact wording was crafted by columnist Lloyd Shearer, writing under his pen name “Walter Scott,” and first published as a set of New Year’s resolutions on the front of Parade magazine on 30 December 1973. Quote Investigator found no Buddhist source for the line, which only began circulating under Buddha’s name around 2013.

source.heading: The documented source

docMeta.dd: A numbered list of New Year’s resolutions on the cover
Gautama Buddha (from c. 2013), George Washington Carver, Ann Landers, and others

source.excerpt: Resolve to be tender with the young, compassionate with the aged, sympathetic with the striving, and tolerant of the weak and the wrong. Sometime in life you will have been all of these.
trail: Quote Investigator dates the complete expression to Parade magazine, 30 December 1973, and concludes Lloyd Shearer “assembled the resolutions and should be credited with crafting the full expression.”
The 1973 printing carried a copyright notice in the name “Walter Scott,” Shearer’s established pen name for “Walter Scott’s Personality Parade”.
Fake Buddha Quotes confirms nothing in the Buddhist canon resembles this line, though it is printed as Buddha’s in at least two books.
Competing later ascriptions — George Washington Carver (a 1982 advertisement) and Ann Landers (1986) — all post-date the 1973 Parade printing, per Quote Investigator.
source.excerptNote: The wording published by Quote Investigator from the 1973 Parade printing. Numerous later variants swap “of the weak and the wrong” for “with the weak and wrong” or open with “How far you go in life depends on…”

source.rightsNote: The exact wording was first published in Parade magazine in 1973 under a “Walter Scott” copyright notice, so in the United States it remains in copyright; the ancient idea of compassion is public, but this specific 20th-century formulation is not.

author.name: Lloyd Shearer
author.heading: Lloyd Shearer
author.bio: Lloyd “Skip” Shearer (1916–2001) was an American celebrity journalist who, under the pen name Walter Scott, wrote the syndicated Q&A feature Walter Scott’s Personality Parade in Parade magazine from 1958 to 1991. It was in that role, in a 1973 New Year’s cover feature, that he composed the list of resolutions now widely misattributed to the Buddha.

misattribution.heading: How Buddha got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a 20th-century American magazine line, not an ancient teaching. It has been pinned on several famous names, all after its true 1973 debut.

items.why: The line began circulating under Buddha’s name only around 2013 and appears in at least two books, but nothing in the Buddhist canon resembles this wording.
Widely credited to Carver (often as “How far you go in life depends on…”), but the earliest Carver ascription is a 1982 advertisement — nearly a decade after Shearer’s 1973 printing.
Ann Landers ran the resolutions in 1986 as a reader submission without attribution, which helped spread the saying without crediting Shearer.

misattribution.truthLine: The complete expression was crafted by Lloyd Shearer (“Walter Scott”) and first published in Parade on 30 December 1973, per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why it spread
lead: The saying has the cadence of scripture — balanced clauses, a turn at the end — which makes it easy to imagine on the lips of a sage. But it was written to fit the front of a Sunday newspaper supplement as one of a set of New Year’s resolutions.

Once the wording detached from Parade, it drifted onto whichever famous name a poster preferred: a scientist, an advice columnist, and eventually the Buddha — the internet’s favorite anonymous-wisdom magnet.
context.pull: A 1973 newspaper resolution, not an ancient sermon.
